SOURCE: "SKILL.state: Scalable Long-Horizon Agent Skills", Sanket Badhe (Google), Priyanka Tiwari (Purdue), Jonghyun Chung (Google). arXiv:2608.26263v3 [cs.AI], dated 2 Sep 2026. Preprint, ACL-style format, no venue stated.

COVERAGE: 46,228 of 46,228 chars read, including all appendices (prompts A, benchmark details B, noise C, extra tables D). The extraction is clean. The PDF carries no page numbers in the text, so "where" below gives section or table. I did not run the figure script. Figure 1 is described only through its extracted labels.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- Claim: Replacing the growing transcript with a three-part prompt (fixed spec, structured JSON state, latest observation) keeps the prompt flat. It keeps accuracy at long horizons and cuts tokens sharply.
  number: At T=100 on Warehouse, SKILL.state scores 0.94 on 65,408 tokens. Stateful (LangGraph-style) scores 0.91 on 1,062,387 tokens, which is 16.2x more.
  setup: SkillExecBench Warehouse, 500 shelves, Gemini-3-Flash, 5 seeds, temperature 0. Authors report p<0.01 (paired t-test) at T≥50.
  quote: "At T= 100 , the Stateful baseline consumes 1,062,387 tokens, whereas SKILL.state consumes only 65,408 to-kens (a 16.2× token reduction)."
  where: §5.2, Table 1

- Claim: At T=200 the history-based runtimes degrade in accuracy while SKILL.state holds. Memory's token cost is about 50x SKILL.state's.
  number: SKILL.state 0.94±0.02 at about 1.8k average prompt chars and 122k tokens. ReAct 0.74, Memory 0.84 (6.18M tokens), Stateful 0.88 (5.04M tokens).
  setup: Same as above.
  quote: "At T= 200 , SKILL.state maintains 0.94 accuracy consuming 122k tokens, while the Memory baseline inflates to 6.1M tokens."
  where: §5.2, Table 1

- Claim: At equal prompt budget, structure beats generic compression. Sliding window, capped summary and LLMLingua all collapse, while the structured state does not.
  number: At T=100, SKILL.state scores 0.94, truncated window 0.18, summary-capped 0.52, ReAct+LLMLingua 0.22. Unbounded ReAct scores 0.84.
  setup: Warehouse, Gemini-3-Flash, budget about 1,800 (the text says both "tokens" and "characters"). 5 seeds.
  quote: "Sliding-window truncation drops to 0.18 because critical early inventory allocations are evicted. LLMLingua drops to 0.22 because statistical en-tropy filtering removes seemingly redundant slot identifiers that are semantically vital."
  where: §5.6, Table 5 and Table 11

- Claim: History-based runtimes keep acting on stale facts after the world changes silently. SKILL.state recovers at once because the corrective alert overwrites the state.
  number: Baselines need 5–8 recovery steps on Warehouse and 8–14 on the Software Repository. SKILL.state needs 0.
  setup: Gemini-3-Flash, hand-built scenarios (secret audit, barcode, move, force push, flaky CI). A cancelled-order and a closed-PR scenario fail for all runtimes.
  quote: "history-based base-lines hallucinate for 5 to 8 consecutive turns be-cause obsolete facts in their prompt history over-power contradictory new observations."
  where: §5.4, Table 3, Table 10

- Claim: Injected distractors hurt the plain transcript runtime badly, but Memory and Stateful are about as robust as SKILL.state.
  number: Prompt (ReAct) falls from 0.68 to 0.53 on Warehouse. SKILL.state stays at 0.97–1.00. On the Software Repository, ReAct falls from 0.76 with no noise to 0.11 at 50 events, and SKILL.state goes 0.90 to 0.80.
  setup: T=50, Gemini-3-Flash, random irrelevant telemetry. 5, 20 or 50 events per turn.
  quote: "the standard Prompt runtime degrades sharply from 0.68 at low noise down to 0.53 at high noise. In contrast, SKILL.state maintains robust task completion (≥0.97 ) across all noise levels"
  where: §5.3, Table 2, Table 9. The text claims SKILL.state is better than the baselines, but Memory scores 1.00 and Stateful 1.00 or 0.98, so the table does not support that.

- Claim: On public benchmarks SKILL.state has the best success rate and the lowest token cost.
  number: InterCode CTF pass@1 54.2% against 46.4% for the best baseline (Memory) and 41.8% for Stateful. Tokens fall 60.4% versus ReAct. τ-Bench Retail 58.3%, Airline 32.4%.
  setup: Gemini-3-Flash. InterCode CTF has 100 tasks. τ-Bench has Retail and Airline. A single static 5-field schema is reused across all CTF tasks (discovered_flags, tested_hypotheses, active_files, working_dir, cmd_summary). Single run, no variance reported.
  quote: "increasing pass@1 to 54.2% (+7.8 points over the strongest baseline and +12.4 points over Stateful) while cutting total tokens by 60.4% vs. ReAct and 65.9% vs. Stateful."
  where: §5.5, Table 4. Retail token saving is small (3.47M against 3.92M for Stateful). The Retail prompt is larger than the baselines' (3,325 against 2,819 and 3,065).

- Claim: SKILL.state's advantage depends on the model. Small open-weight models gain less and fail by corrupting state.
  number: Gemma-4-31B at T=100 scores 0.42, tied with Stateful at 0.42. Qwen-3-8B at T=100 scores 0.34 against Stateful's 0.31. Errors: 68% premature overwrite or deletion, 20% schema/type coercion, 12% JSON syntax.
  setup: Warehouse, Tables 7–8, T=100. The error taxonomy is for Gemma-4-31B.
  quote: "Premature State Overwrite / Deletion (68%):The model accidentally omits existing keys dur-ing state update rather than merging in-place."
  where: §5.7, Tables 7–8

- Claim: The design discards chain-of-thought after each step and keeps only a validated state patch. Prompt length is bounded and cumulative cost is linear instead of quadratic. This is an asymptotic argument, not a measurement.
  number: O(1) prompt, O(T) cumulative against O(T²) for transcripts.
  setup: Section 3. The runtime validates the patch deterministically, applies a dictionary merge with null-deletes, then executes the action. An invalid patch triggers rollback and retry.
  quote: "Σt+1 = Σt ⊕∆Σ t,(4) where ⊕ denotes the runtime's dictionary merge operator with null-deletion semantics."
  where: §3.2–3.3, Algorithm 1

- Claim: Software Repository results are weaker. SKILL.state wins at long horizons but loses to Stateful at T=25.
  number: T=25: SKILL.state 0.88 against Stateful 0.94. T=100: SKILL.state 0.78 against Stateful 0.63.
  setup: Gemini-3-Flash, 5 seeds.
  where: Table 6

LIMITS
- The authors concede the whole approach rests on state being a "sufficient statistic". It fails when:
  - the schema is unknown in advance;
  - an observation's relevance is not recognised when first seen, so it never enters the state;
  - the task is about the history itself, such as auditing or provenance.
- It is single-agent only. Multi-agent use is untested and would need conflict-resolution rules in the merge operator.
- Small models need grammar-constrained decoding. This is stated as future work and was not tested.
- My observations on the evidence:
  - Everything uses one frontier model (Gemini-3-Flash) for the headline results, and the open-weight results are weaker.
  - The synthetic benchmark was built by the authors. Its tasks (a 500-slot inventory and a Git simulator) suit an explicit key-value state.
  - The Stateful baseline keeps the full transcript and adds a state block, so it is not an "ablate the transcript" comparison.
  - Public-benchmark results have no variance or seeds.
  - The budget is given as both tokens and characters.
  - The text says Airline baseline prompts "peak above 11,000 tokens/step", but Table 4 shows 4,700–5,400. These may be different statistics, but it is not reconciled.
  - The state schema is hand-authored per domain. No cost or effort is reported.
  - There is no latency measurement, even though the abstract mentions latency.

BUILDS ON
- ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) as the baseline.
- MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023), Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023), Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2023/2024) and Wang et al. 2023 as the memory lineage it departs from.
- LangGraph, for "auxiliary structured state".
- Dialogue state tracking (Williams et al., 2013; Henderson et al., 2014; Rastogi et al., 2020 schema-guided dialogue).
- LLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2023) and Li et al., 2023 for compression.
- Lost in the Middle (Liu et al., 2024) and ∞Bench (Zhang et al., 2024) for long-context degradation.
- InterCode (Yang et al., 2023) and τ-bench (Yao et al., 2024) as benchmarks.
- The authors' own skills survey (Badhe et al., 2026) and skill-security paper (Badhe and Tiwari, 2026, arXiv:2607.13987).

CODE
- Appendix A.4, the SKILL.state prompt (verbatim):
  `Skill Execution State: {json.dumps(state, separators=(',',':'))} Latest Observation: {observation}`. The model is asked for "1. Step-by-step reasoning (will be discarded after execution) 2. A JSON block ... exactly these two keys: { "state_patch": { <dict: your state updates, set keys to null to delete> }, "action": "<string: the exact command you want to execute>" }".
- Appendix B.3, an example patch: `{"state_patch": {"inventory": {"shelf_42": null}}, "action": "Ship item_12 shelf_42"}`.
- Algorithm 1 loop: observe, build prompt (P, Σt, Ot), generate (Rt, ΔΣt, at), validate ΔΣt, Σt+1 = Σt ⊕ ΔΣt, execute at.

FIGURES: Figure 1 (§3) compares the two runtimes. The traditional one has an O(T) prompt with history. SKILL.state has an O(1) prompt, discards reasoning, and applies a JSON-patch update. Its panels plot prompt size against steps, rising versus flat. Check the figure directly before reusing it.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- No page numbers in the extraction.
- The author list shows a trailing comma after Chung, with no further authors.
- The reference list has duplicate entries (Xiao 2024a/b, Zhong 2023/2024).
- Some table cells run together in extraction (for example "0.90±0.023,249±949,438±371" is 0.90±0.02, 3,249±94, 9,438±371).
- The Appendix D heading ".1 / .2" is garbled.

FIT TO THE COURSE
- Best fit is notes/07-structured-context.md. It supports structured state (a schema'd JSON object, patch updates, validated by the runtime) as a replacement for transcript replay. The Budget-Matched Controls table (Table 5) is the most useful single result: structure beats truncation, capped summary and LLMLingua at the same size.
- It also supports 05-compression-compaction.md (a counterpoint to summaries and compression) and 11-failure-modes.md (stale facts and context poisoning, the state-recovery experiment).
- It is only loosely about "skills". The paper uses "skill" for any procedure the agent runs and says nothing about skill files, loading or discovery, so it has little relevance to 02 Layer 2 or 04 Just-in-time context.
- Overall it is a modest, usable single-lab preprint with an author-built benchmark and one main model. Cite it as evidence for the pattern, with the caveats above (sufficient-statistic assumption, small-model fragility, single run on public benchmarks).
